q: The Preamble of the Constitution of India is based on:
options: The Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru
explanation: The Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution, moved by Nehru on 13 Dec 1946 and adopted 22 Jan 1947. The GoI Act 1935 supplied administrative machinery (not ideals); the Nehru Report (1928) proposed dominion status; the Cabinet Mission created the Assembly, not the Preamble.

q: The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' were added to the Preamble by which amendment?
explanation: The 42nd Amendment (1976) — the 'Mini-Constitution' — added all three words; it remains the only amendment ever made to the Preamble. The 44th (1978) reversed several 42nd changes but left the Preamble untouched. The 52nd is anti-defection; the 24th clarified amendability of FRs.

q: In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble:
options: Is not a part of the Constitution
Is enforceable in courts of law
Is a part of the Constitution
explanation: Berubari (1960): the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution; it is a key to the makers' minds. This was overruled in Kesavananda (1973), which made it a part. Option C is wrong in both cases; option D was never held — the Preamble is non-justiciable.

q: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court held that:
options: The Preamble is part of the Constitution and can be amended without altering the basic structure
The Preamble cannot be amended under any circumstances
The Preamble is not part of the Constitution
explanation: Kesavananda held the Preamble IS part of the Constitution and CAN be amended (Art 368's proviso applies), but the basic structure — which the Preamble's ideals define — cannot be destroyed. Option A is Berubari (1960); option D is nonsense — the Preamble is non-justiciable.

q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched? (Preamble element — Interpretation)
options: Secular — the State has no religion of its own; equal respect to all
Sovereign — dominion status within the Commonwealth
Socialist — communistic state ownership of all industry
explanation: Secularism here is positive secularism (Sarva Dharma Samabhava) — the State has no official religion and treats all equally (S.R. Bommai, 1994). Option A is wrong: Indian socialism is democratic socialism (mixed economy), not communism. Option C: a republic has an elected head. Option D: sovereignty means free of external control — Commonwealth membership does not limit it.

q: The correct chronological order of ideals as they appear in the Preamble is:
explanation: The Preamble order: Justice (social, economic, political) → Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship) → Equality (status, opportunity) → Fraternity (dignity + unity & integrity). Mnemonic JLEF. BPSC loves order-scrambling traps.

q: 'Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship' in the Preamble is reflected in which set of Fundamental Rights?
explanation: Liberty of thought/expression → Art 19 (speech etc.) and the Art 20–22 cluster; belief/faith/worship → Arts 25–28 (freedom of religion). Arts 14–18 embody equality; Arts 29–30 cultural/educational rights; Arts 23–24 abolition of exploitation.

q: The phrase 'economic justice' in the Preamble is primarily reflected in:
options: Part XII — Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits
Part IV — Directive Principles of State Policy
explanation: Economic and social justice is the domain of DPSP (Part IV) — the SC in D.S. Nakara (1982) linked the Preamble's economic justice to DPSPs (e.g., Art 39). FRs secure political justice primarily; Part IVA is duties; Part XII is financial administration.

q: Consider the following statements about the Preamble: 1. It is non-justiciable — not enforceable in a court of law. 2. It is a legitimate aid in interpreting ambiguous provisions of the Constitution. 3. It was amended once, by the 42nd Amendment, 1976. Which is/are correct?
explanation: All three are correct. Non-justiciable but a valid interpretive aid (used in Kesavananda, Bommai); amended once only (42nd, 1976 — Socialist, Secular, Integrity).

q: The Preamble declares India to be:
explanation: Today's text: 'SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC' — five descriptors in order. Option A is the 1949–1976 text. Option D inserts 'Federal' — the Preamble does not use the word 'federal' (India is a 'Union of States', Art 1).

q: The ideal of 'Justice — social, economic, political' in the Preamble is inspired by:
explanation: The ideal of justice (social, economic, political) comes from the Russian Revolution. Liberty, equality, fraternity come from the French Revolution. The Irish gave DPSP. US gave FRs/judicial review.

q: 'Fraternity' in the Preamble means:
options: The dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation
A band of brothers in arms against the State
explanation: Fraternity assures the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation ('integrity' added by the 42nd). Option C is economic justice/equality; option D is liberty of faith/worship. Art 51A(e) is its statutory echo.

q: In November 2024, the Supreme Court (in Balram Singh v. Union of India) held that:
options: 'Socialist' and 'secular' must be deleted from the Preamble
The 1976 insertion of 'socialist' and 'secular' in the Preamble is valid and the words remain
The Preamble's text can be amended only by a Constituent Assembly
The Preamble is not part of the Constitution
explanation: The SC dismissed the petition to delete 'socialist'/'secular': Parliament's Art 368 power extends to the Preamble (42nd Amendment precedent; Kesavananda), and the insertion stands. Option C contradicts Kesavananda; option D is wrong — ordinary Art 368 procedure applies.

q: The Preamble states that the Constitution was adopted 'in our Constituent Assembly' on:
explanation: The Preamble's final line records adoption on 'this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949' — unchanged even after the 42nd Amendment. 26 Jan 1950 is commencement; 9 Dec 1946 is the first sitting. The adoption/commencement distinction is a BPSC staple.

q: Which of the following is NOT a descriptor used for India in the Preamble?
explanation: The Preamble does not describe India as 'federal' (Art 1: 'Union of States'; the country is federal in structure but the word is absent — Ambedkar's deliberate choice). Socialist/Secular (42nd), Republic (from 1949) all appear.

q: Match List-I (Preamble term) with List-II (closest constitutional embodiment): (a) Justice, social (b) Liberty of worship (c) Equality of opportunity (d) Fraternity — 1) Art 25 2) Art 15(4) 3) Art 46 4) Art 51A(e)
explanation: Justice-social → Art 46 (weaker sections); liberty of worship → Art 25 (freedom of conscience); equality of opportunity → Art 15(4)/16(4); fraternity → Art 51A(e). Matching Preamble ideals to specific Articles is a high-yield BPSC pattern.

q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the Preamble?
options: It embodies the basic structure of the Constitution's ideals
It is a part of the Constitution
It is enforceable in courts of law
explanation: The Preamble is non-justiciable — no one can enforce it in court; it is interpretive material only. (A) is right post-Kesavananda; (C) is right (42nd precedent); (D) is right — the SC uses it to identify basic-structure elements (e.g., secularism in Bommai).

q: The Preamble's phrase 'We, the people of India' signifies:
options: Only citizens who ratified the Constitution in a referendum
Popular sovereignty — ultimate authority lies with the people of India
The Constituent Assembly was directly elected by all adults
The Constitution is made by the representatives, not the people
explanation: 'We, the people' proclaims popular sovereignty: the Constitution derives from the people. There was no referendum (option C) and the Assembly was indirectly elected (option D — the classic CA trap, see Topic 38).

q: Thakurdas Bhargava described the Preamble as:
options: The identity card of the Constitution
The horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic
explanation: Thakurdas Bhargava: 'the horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'; K.M. Munshi: 'political horoscope'. N.A. Palkhivala called it the 'identity card of the Constitution'. The tested pairing is horoscope → Bhargava.

q: Consider the following pairs (word added — amendment): 1. Socialist — 42nd 2. Secular — 42nd 3. Integrity — 44th 4. Democratic — 42nd. Which are correctly matched?
explanation: Socialist, Secular AND Integrity were ALL added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — pair 3 is wrong (44th did not touch the Preamble); pair 4 is wrong because 'Democratic' was in the original 1949 text.

q: The Preamble is silent on which of the following?
options: The date of commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950)
The source of authority for the Constitution
The nature of the State (democratic, socialist etc.)
explanation: The Preamble mentions the adoption date (26 Nov 1949), NOT the commencement date (26 Jan 1950). Source of authority, nature of State and objectives are all there.

q: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that secularism:
options: Is a basic feature of the Constitution
Applies only to the Union, not the States
Was inserted in the Preamble in 1994
Means the State must be anti-religion
explanation: Bommai (1994): secularism is a basic feature; misuse of religion by a State government can invite Art 356 action. 'Secular' entered the Preamble in 1976 (42nd), not 1994. Indian secularism = positive/equal respect, NOT anti-religion; it binds both Union and States.

q: Which pair is NOT correctly matched? (Preamble ideal — Source of inspiration)
explanation: Fraternity comes from the French Revolution (fraternité), not the Russian. Justice (social-economic-political) is the Russian contribution; liberty and equality are French.

q: The 42nd Amendment is called the 'Mini-Constitution' because it: 1. Added words to the Preamble 2. Added Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) 3. Added new Directive Principles (Arts 43A, 48A) 4. Curtailed judicial review
explanation: All four: Preamble words, Fundamental Duties (Art 51A, USSR model), new DPSPs (43A, 48A), and curtailment of judicial review — hence 'Mini-Constitution'. The 44th (1978) reversed only parts.

q: 'Equality of status and of opportunity' in the Preamble corresponds most closely to which constitutional provision?
options: Articles 14, 15, 16 and the DPSP Art 39 (equal pay etc.)
Article 21 — protection of life and personal liberty
explanation: Equality of status → Arts 14–15; equality of opportunity → Art 16 and DPSP Art 39. Art 21 is liberty; Art 32 is remedies; Art 51A is duties.
